extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers, grant reviewers, funding-agency administrators and policy-makers concerned with fairness in peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and study of the peer-review scoring system used by a biomedical funding agency for postdoctoral fellowship applications, including the scoring parameters, productivity measures, and non-scientific factors that influence reviewers' competence ratings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific competence
rubrics_metrics.description: One of three parameters rated by each reviewer (score between 0 and 4); considered related to number and quality of scientific publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers gave female applicants lower average scientific competence scores (2.21 vs 2.46). The authors used multiple-regression analyses to relate competence scores to productivity variables; gender and reviewer affiliation remained significant predictors even after controlling for productivity. Scientific competence scores are multiplied with the other two parameter scores to form a product score (see product score).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance of the research proposal
rubrics_metrics.description: One of three parameters rated by each reviewer on a 0–4 scale reflecting how relevant the proposed research is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included in the product score calculation; female applicants received slightly lower average relevance scores (2.49 vs 2.62). No separate productivity-based model was shown for this parameter, but it contributes multiplicatively to final ranking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of the proposed methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: One of three parameters rated by each reviewer on a 0–4 scale assessing methodological quality of the proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included in the product score; female applicants scored lower on average (2.37 vs 2.54). Methodological quality is treated equally with competence and relevance in the scoring system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product score (multiplicative combination of three parameter scores)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each reviewer’s three parameter scores (scientific competence, relevance, methodology) are multiplied to yield a product score ranging from 0 to 64.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The multiplicative scoring amplifies small differences across parameters, leading to substantial differences in final product scores between applicants with modest parameter score differences. The average of five reviewers' product scores is used as the applicant's final score for ranking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final average score and committee ranking
rubrics_metrics.description: The final score for each applicant is the average of five reviewers' product scores; applicants are then ranked within each evaluation committee and fellowships are usually awarded to the top-ranked applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fellowships were distributed based on rank within a committee rather than absolute score values; committee-to-committee differences in stingency therefore do not necessarily change a candidate's chance relative to their committee peers. The MRC board makes the ultimate award decisions, typically choosing one to three top-ranked applicants per committee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total number of original scientific publications
rubrics_metrics.description: A productivity variable measured from the applicant’s bibliography (double-checked with Medline).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as one of six productivity measures to assess whether competence ratings matched scientific productivity. Provided as a straightforward count metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total number of first-author publications
rubrics_metrics.description: A productivity variable counting papers on which the applicant is first author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to reflect independent scientific contribution; analyzed in regression models to predict competence scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total impact (sum of journals' impact factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: A productivity measure constructed by adding the impact factors of the journals in which the applicant's papers were published; unit = impact points (one impact point = one paper in a journal with impact factor 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This measure produced the regression model with highest explanatory power (r2 = 0.47). The authors translate impact-point differences into approximate equivalent numbers of high-impact papers (e.g., ~64 impact points ≈ three Nature/Science papers or ~20 papers in journals with impact factor ≈3). Used to quantify how much extra productivity women needed to equal men's competence scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-author impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Sum of the impact factors of journals in which the applicant’s first-author papers appeared (measured in impact points).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included as one of six productivity variables; regression model based on this measure yielded results similar to the total-impact model regarding gender and affiliation effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total citations (during a specified year)
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of times the applicant's scientific papers were cited during 1994 (used here as 'total citations').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a productivity metric; one of the models (first-author citations and total citations) had predictive power and yielded similar conclusions about gender and affiliation effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-author citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of times papers on which the applicant was first author were cited during 1994.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a productivity variable in regression analyses and showed similar patterns to the impact-based measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant gender
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-scientific factor (male/female) found to have a significant independent influence on competence scores in multiple-regression models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Male applicants received a 'male gender' bonus (about +0.21 competence points in the total-impact model). Women needed substantially higher productivity (e.g., ~64 impact points more) to receive the same competence score as male colleagues. The article presents this as evidence of gender-based discrimination in peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affiliation with a committee member (reviewer affiliation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the applicant was affiliated with any of the members of the evaluation committee (noted on protocols); reviewers with such ties are not allowed to participate in scoring that applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite recusal rules, applicants affiliated with committee members received an 'affiliation bonus' (~+0.22 competence points), equivalent to ~67 impact points. Neutral reviewers appear to compensate by raising scores for affiliated applicants. Affiliation could offset the gender penalty for women in aggregate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letter of recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of a letter of recommendation accompanying the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Had a positive effect on competence scores in the model based on total impact, but not in the two other productivity-based models — i.e., effect inconsistent across specifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation committee assignment (committee stingency)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specific evaluation committee to which an applicant was assigned; committees differed in how 'stern' they were in evaluating competence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee identity influenced absolute competence scores (some committees were stricter), but because fellowships were awarded by rank within committees, assignment to a 'tough' committee did not change an applicant's chance of award relative to committee peers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nationality, basic education, scientific field, postdoctoral experience abroad
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant background factors examined (Swedish/non-Swedish nationality; basic education: medical, science or nursing; scientific field; postdoc experience abroad) for influence on competence scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors did not significantly influence competence scores in the models tested, suggesting they were not primary determinants in this dataset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secrecy versus transparency of peer-review scores
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy dimension concerning whether reviewer evaluation scores should be made public (secrecy had previously prevented study of scores).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors argue secrecy must be abandoned to allow scientific evaluation of peer-review systems; Swedish Freedom of the Press Act allowed access to scores and enabled this study. Concerns that openness would drive reviewers away appear exaggerated, as reviewer participation remained after scores became accessible in Sweden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict-of-interest handling and its limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing policy: reviewers who are affiliated with applicants are not allowed to participate in scoring those applicants (affiliation noted on protocols).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although formal recusal rules existed, they were insufficient because neutral reviewers compensated by inflating scores for affiliated applicants — showing that simple recusal rules do not eliminate nepotism effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer demographics and potential effects (reviewer gender distribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: The composition of reviewers (e.g., only 5 of 55 reviewers were female) and its possible effect on scoring behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small number and uneven distribution of female reviewers prevented statistical analysis of their scoring behavior in this study. Prior studies suggest female evaluators may be more objective when assessing women, but the authors caution that simply increasing female reviewers might not fully solve discrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: System-level vulnerabilities: inter-reviewer reliability and reviewer bias
rubrics_metrics.description: General critiques of peer review, including poor inter-reviewer reliability and tendency of reviewers to favor confirmatory work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study provides empirical evidence that peer review is susceptible to nepotism and prejudice. The authors call for development of peer-review systems with built-in resistance to human biases and for more empirical studies across countries and disciplines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of statistical evaluation (multiple-regression) to assess scoring determinants
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological criterion: apply multiple-regression models relating competence scores to productivity measures and candidate/committee characteristics to identify primary influences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Six separate regression models (one per productivity variable) were used; three produced statistically significant models (total impact, first-author impact, first-author citations). The regression approach permits elimination of confounding factors and quantifies effect sizes (e.g., r2, intercepts, impact-point equivalents). The authors recommend similar empirical analyses be conducted in other systems.
